desc:
You are given n nodes labelled 0 to n - 1 and a list of undirected edges, where edges[i] = [a, b] connects a and b.

Return true if these edges form a tree on all n nodes: every node can reach every other node, and there is no cycle. Otherwise return false.

n = 5, edges = [[0,1],[0,2],[0,3],[1,4]]   result = true
n = 5, edges = [[0,1],[1,2],[2,3],[1,3],[1,4]]   result = false  (1-2-3 is a cycle)
n = 4, edges = [[0,1],[2,3]]   result = false  (two separate pieces)
constraints: 0 ≤ a, b < n and a ≠ b
No pair of nodes appears twice
hints: Count the edges first. How many edges does a tree on n nodes have?
A tree has exactly n - 1 edges. With that many edges, the graph is a tree if it is connected, and also if it has no cycle: either property implies the other.

Union the endpoints of each edge. If an edge ever joins two nodes that already have the same root, there is a cycle, so return false. After all edges, a graph with n - 1 edges and no cycle is automatically connected.
editorial: Two cheap facts decide everything. A tree on n nodes has exactly n - 1 edges, so any other edge count is an immediate false. When the count is right, "connected" and "acyclic" are equivalent, so checking one is enough.

Run union-find over the edges. If some edge connects two nodes that already share a root, it closes a cycle and the answer is false. If all n - 1 unions succeed, every union merged two different components, so n nodes shrink to n - (n - 1) = 1 component and the graph is a tree. Time is O(n + m · α(n)); a DFS that checks connectivity gives the same result.
